tags.gist: Endorses the two-axis risk framework as something the paper got right that should carry into policy.
Endorses judging directiveness by an output's substance and setting rather than wording, with a talk-to-your-doctor disclaimer not reducing it.
Endorses judging risk over realistic conversational trajectories spanning many turns rather than isolated outputs.
Endorses evaluating the deployed device configuration rather than the foundation model in isolation.
Endorses requiring adjudicators, including LLM adjudicators, to be structurally independent from sponsor and model developer.
Endorses treating both directions of escalation, refusal and deferral error as failures, and a subgroup definition covering dialect and literacy.
Endorses the paper's candor about benchmark contamination, synthetic-data circularity and developers' weak incentive to disclose.
Would make data exposure a dimension of risk, since where patient inputs go, their retention and training use, and patient disclosure should count.
Would not trade premarket evidence for monitoring outside the lowest-risk quadrant, and only with a GenAI reporting taxonomy, public thresholds and a patient channel.
Would make foundation model transparency mandatory, or else place the full evidence burden on the sponsor, with public model cards for marketed devices.
Wants version pinning, contractual change notice, no silent updates and re-benchmarking of any new version before patients see it; a PCCP cannot cover uncontrolled changes.
Says the credentialing analogy justifies competency testing but breaks on identity, accountability, scale and self-knowledge, so evidence should bind to a fixed configuration.
Would hold benchmarking to bench-testing standards: distributional reporting, different-lineage synthetic data, different-family LLM judges and sequestered datasets.
Wants the standard of care, not the median clinician, as comparator, and team evaluation that measures automation bias.
Says under-escalation is irreversible while over-escalation is recoverable, so the trade-off should be prespecified, disclosed and weighted toward safety.
Says machine supervisors may sort cases for review but cannot stand in for human review.
Wants agentic devices to require human sign-off ahead of irreversible actions, immutable audit logs and hard tool boundaries.
Supports patient-facing access with disclosure that the user faces a machine, plain-language limits, data-flow disclosure and a path to reach a person.
States three guiding principles: resolve tensions for the patient, hold evaluation to bench-testing science, and treat data protection as a safety property.
Calls the activity-by-consequence framework a sound organizing heuristic.
Supports judging directiveness by substance and context, and holding that a disclaimer only shifts responsibility to the person least able to evaluate the instruction.
Supports assessing risk across conversational trajectories and treating cumulative out-of-scope drift as a boundary failure, calling it ahead of other regulators.
Calls evaluating the configured user-facing device, not the foundation model, the paper's most important sentence, reinforced by master files not authorizing a model.
Supports structural independence of adjudicators from sponsor and model developer, even where an LLM does the adjudicating.
Supports attention to both directions of escalation, refusal and deferral error, broad subgroup performance including dialect and literacy, and naming automation bias.
Values the paper's candor about benchmark contamination, same-class synthetic data, developers' weak incentive to disclose, and medical paternalism.
Would make data exposure a third axis or mandatory modifier, covering whether inputs leave the sponsor, are retained, train models, or are disclosed to patients.
Wants sponsors to document a function's data flow and, for patient-facing functions, treat a ban on using device inputs for training as a minimum safeguard.
Gives a qualified no: reduced premarket evidence fits only non-directive, low-consequence functions; elsewhere it shifts risk from sponsor to patient.
Would make data exposure a third axis or mandatory modifier, covering whether inputs leave the sponsor, are retained, train models, or are disclosed.
Cautions that shared responsibility must not diffuse accountability: others contribute signal, but the sponsor remains responsible, including for licensed components.
Proposes a rule: developer documentation reaches FDA, or else the sponsor must treat the model as a black box and carry the full evidence burden.
Would make the model or system card for any model in a marketed device public, since its limitations are labeling, not trade secrets.
Calls a PCCP the wrong instrument for uncontrolled changes and would require version pinning, notice periods, no silent updates and re-benchmarking before use.
Accepts the credentialing analogy for structured assessment and supervised practice, but says it breaks in four places with regulatory consequences.
Says a model can be silently replaced where a clinician cannot, so competency evidence must bind to an immutable configuration and any change triggers reassessment.
Says the paper proposes no accountability mechanism and wants a prespecified, trigger-based route to suspend a device's authorization, faster than a recall.
Argues acceptance criteria for safety-critical behaviors should be stricter than for one practitioner, since a systematic error hits every patient at once.
Says a model's stated uncertainty is itself generated, so deferral should be tested adversarially across paraphrases and not accepted as a safeguard on its say-so.
Would adopt the framework for what the analogy supports and explicitly reject invoking it to loosen change control or spread accountability.
Strongly supports prespecified methods and criteria and would extend the parallel with bench testing in four ways.
Wants performance reported as a distribution with disclosed decoding settings, and variation in safety-critical behavior treated as a firm acceptance failure.
Wants synthetic data from a different lineage, never the sole basis for subgroup claims, with its share reported and concordance shown before combining.
Wants LLM adjudicators from a different model family, checked against human adjudicators on held-out cases with agreement reported and disclosed.
Supports sequestered datasets held by third parties the sponsor never sees, with sponsor benchmarks not the sole gate, under an ASCA-like multi-body model.
Rejects the median clinician as normalizing care gaps; wants the standard of care as floor, specialist comparators for specialist questions, and automation-bias measurement.
Calls escalation errors asymmetric and wants the trade-off prespecified, disclosed in labeling, and not loosened on emergency department cost arguments.
Says a supervisory agent shares the device's failure modes, may triage but not replace human review, and needs independent validation first.
Wants agentic devices to have a mandatory human checkpoint before irreversible actions, an immutable audit log, and a tested boundary on tools.
Supports patient-facing access given machine disclosure, plain labeling, data-flow disclosure and a route to a human, moving functions up only when these are absent.
Calls the paper serious and forward-looking and asks CDRH to carry its commitments through, including data exposure as safety and transparency as a condition.
